newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon concerned over new arrest in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon concerned over new arrest in Japan.

text.p: The U.S. Defence Department on Thursday expressed concern at an American airman's alleged break-in of a woman's apartment in Okinawa but said this did not compare to the 1995 rape of a Japanese schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.

"We are concerned, the secretary (Defense Secretary William Cohen) is very disturbed by anything that violates the standards of good manners and good neighbours and good discipline," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters.
"This is, of course, not at all comparable to earlier well-publicised problems in Okinawa. This seems to be a different situation," he added.

Bacon spoke a day after a U.S. Air Force sergeant was arrested on indecency and illegal entry charges for allegedly breaking into a woman's apartment in Okinawa, the latest suspected crime by U.S. military personnel in Japan.

"We are worried about any action by any American military personnel that violates American standards of behaviour or Japanese laws. I think we have to wait and see what the allegations or charges are here, how this turns out," Bacon said.
The September 1995 rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen triggered widespread protests against the huge U.S. military presence on Okinawa.
Okinawa police spokesman Katsuya Matayoshi said investigators arrested Staff Sgt. Danny Matlock, 33, on Wednesday and charged him with indecent exposure as well as breaking and entering.
Matlock was suspected of entering a 28-year-old Okinawan woman's house in Okinawa city shortly after midnight early on Monday, the spokesman said.

The incident could be another blow to the image of the U.S. military in Japan following the arrest of an American sailor at Yokosuka Naval Base 15 miles (24 km) south of Tokyo earlier this month on suspicion of beating and sexually assaulting his Japanese girlfriend in his quarters.
Okinawa is home to half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan and hosts more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan.
U.S. Air Force military police helped Okinawa police in the latest case, Japanese police said.
Kadena U.S. Air Force Base spokesman Chris Ames said Japanese police were handling the case as the airman was living off the base.
Bacon was asked about Cohen's repeated reminder to U.S. troops during a visit to Japan this month that they were "ambassadors" of the United States as well as military personnel.
"We will continue to train our troops," responded Bacon.

"But people are not perfect. Life is not perfect. We face challenges every day, and we will continue to do our absolute best through training, through example, through exortation, to ensure that our military personnel both abroad and in the United States follow the absolute highest standards of behaviour."
